extracted.intended_audience: readers and students interested in the dramatic art, actors, and theatrical history
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the psychological origin, varieties, and personal uses of the dramatic art, aimed at explaining what drama is, how it appears in nature and society, and what makes effective or harmful dramatic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeing life dramatically / interpretive habit
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of seeing people and things group themselves in pictures, of looking on scenes and acts in their relationship as a whole, of reading character and getting at states of mind and plucking out personal secrets by an intuitive and cultivated art of interpreting the signs consciously or unconsciously given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This faculty imparts keener, more diversified, more comprehensive interest to experience; it is characteristic of highest artistic genius (Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Goethe). Cultivate the ability to 'read' signs and to view scenes holistically; it is the basis for dramatic understanding beyond mere textual knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that drama exists beyond the play-house
rubrics_metrics.description: The Theatre, technically so called, is but one of the lesser spheres of the dramatic art; every spot in which man meets his fellow-men is a secondary theatre, arrayed with its scenery of circumstances, where each has his rôle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit appreciation of acting to staged performances; practice and evaluation of dramatic ability should include everyday social interplay, where roles, masks, and back-stage dynamics occur. Teaching and critique should therefore consider naturalistic, social acting as part of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy and contagion as basis of dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic elements arise from crude instincts of intelligence, imagination, and sympathy: seeing signals of inner states in others produces the same states in oneself (sympathetic contagion exemplified by panics in animals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and use the mechanics of sympathetic response (attitudes, movements, cries, nervous contractions) to produce believable dramatic effects. Examples from animal behavior (herds, birds) illustrate how outward signs communicate inner states rapidly; effective acting elicits similar sympathetic response in audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mimetic (barbaric) vs creative (child) dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Barbaric dramatization is mimetic—putting on from without the disguise, posture, sounds of the animal impersonated; child dramatization is creative—a projection from within of the child's own thoughts and emotions into personified objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing dramatic work, note whether performance is merely imitative (external signs without inner creative life) or genuinely projects inner experience outward. Creative projection is morally and artistically superior; training should aim to develop inward imaginative projection rather than mere surface mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three provinces of savage drama and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Among rudest tribes the drama has three provinces: (1) reenactments of actual life incidents (festivals, war), (2) impersonations of animals (Eagle Dance, Wolf Dance), (3) impersonations of supernatural beings; these practices give vividness but can also degrade or inflame ferocity and superstition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of ritual or animal impersonation can provide cultural energy and vividness but beware of its anti-social or pathological effects: practices that reinforce bestial traits or long, spasmodic ritual can deepen degradation, ferocity, and even insanity. In producing drama, aim to avoid reinforcing baser instincts and to promote higher human types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fables as a distinct dramatic device (didactic dramatization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fables combine childlike projection and barbaric inversion: animals are given human souls to teach moral truths; the author puts his human nature into humbler creatures with a deliberate didactic purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing anthropomorphic dramatization, be deliberate about moral lessons and reflective distance. Fable-drama is creative and pedagogical—evaluate success by clarity of lesson and imaginative fidelity rather than mere mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art versus instinct: repeatability and conscious representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower animals may dramatize for practical ends (feigning death, mimicry), but human art differs in being able to repeat the serial action under other circumstances and to perform consciously before an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True dramatic art requires conscious, repeatable performance and reflective control; training should emphasize the actor's ability to reproduce and adapt performances intentionally rather than relying on spontaneous instinct alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical presence and vocal articulation as actor virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The mature actor's qualities include massive majesty of pose, slow weight of gesture, fixedness of look, ponderous gutturality and sweetness of articulative energy, intensity and equilibrium of selfhood—producing personal magnetism and the power to attract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actors on stage presence (pose, gesture, look), vocal qualities (range, timbre, articulation), and the inner balance of selfhood (intensity without loss of equilibrium). Training should develop body, voice, and the charismatic coherence of personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship and gradual professional development
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice (from Cooper): do not trust raw triumphs as an amateur; be willing to serve a regular apprenticeship, climb the ladder round by round, begin in relatively humble parts and grow by degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For aspiring actors: accept modest beginnings, learn all experiences of the profession, be studious and modest. Avoid attempts to 'mount by great skips'; progression through varied practical roles builds durable skill and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic art as a means to uplift by exemplary types
rubrics_metrics.description: When a superior stranger or inspired genius presents a new style of man, the multitude copies it; the appearance of an inspired superior whose characteristics are imitated is the dynamic essence of social progress (and 'the dynamic essence of Christianity itself').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use drama to present elevated human types for emulation; evaluate dramatic works by whether they offer models that can ethically and culturally uplift audiences rather than merely entertain or degrade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of dramatic practice that emphasize bestiality or superstition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolonged impersonation of lower creatures or of fiendish supernatural beings tends to animalize actors, submitting the brain to lower centres and furnishing conditions for insanity and besotted superstition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dramatic practices that involve prolonged, convulsive, or rhythmically excessive mimicry of destructive passions; ethically review such material for potential harmful psychological effects on performers and communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of early imaginative play in developing dramatic faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's nurseries and play (dolls, toy soldiers) function as theatres where the child is author, manager, actor, and spectator, projecting life into toys and prefiguring later dramatic capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage imaginative play in youth as foundational training for dramatic sensibility; evaluate early dramatic aptitude by richness of imaginative projection and role-play rather than technical polish.
